# A proposed approach: scanning the glandular tissue {#sec-on-the-fly} @sec-tumour-size concludes that we need to measure the glandular, less fatty tissue. This section proposes one way of doing that. What we need is a rule we could apply **at the instrument, while measuring**, to decide whether a scan is good enough to use. To be fair it must meet three conditions: 1. **Blind.** It uses only the scan itself, never the breast's label or the result of the comparison. 2. **Symmetric.** It is applied the same way to both breasts, so neither is favoured. 3. **Fixed in advance.** Its threshold is set before the comparison is made, not tuned to give the best result. Each breast is scanned a few times, usually three, and some of those scans will miss the glandular tissue. So the rule works scan by scan: - **A scan is usable** if it has a real water peak: its water peak height (the mean of its prepared curve over q = 20-22) is at least **0.35**, that is 35% of the fat peak's height, and its fitted water Gaussian is centred at **q ≥ 19**, so the fit has found a water peak and not just the shoulder of the fat peak. - **A breast is usable** if at least one of its scans is; its Water:Fat comes from the mean of its usable scans only. - **A patient is compared** only if **both** breasts are usable. ::: {.callout-important title="Using the water peak as a filter during scanning"} The filter can be applied while the patient is on the instrument, but not in a single step. At each position it needs: 1. **A short scan**, long enough to see the fat and water peaks. 2. **A quick analysis** of that scan: correct the peak position, normalise, and measure the water peak against the fat peak (water peak height ≥ 0.35 of the fat peak, water centred at q ≥ 19). 3. **A decision**: if the scan has a real water peak, the position is in glandular tissue and the full scan **proceeds**; if not, the operator **moves to another spot** and repeats from step 1. So the scanning software would need this analysis built in, between the short scan and the full scan, much like the existing transmission check (Phase 1) that decides whether a position is scanned. In theory, this could be implemented on Human 1.0. ::: ::: {#cell-fig-on-the-fly-example .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # WATER_MIN, CENTRE_MIN, scan_records, usable, rule_breasts, rule_results and rule_text come from cohort_common all_scans_results = rule_results(-np.inf, -np.inf) # every scan used: the result of @fig-all-patients rule = rule_results(WATER_MIN, CENTRE_MIN) usable_share = np.mean([usable(h, c, WATER_MIN, CENTRE_MIN) for *_, h, c in scan_records]) # an example: the first CANCER/NORMAL patient the rule compares in which each breast has both usable and rejected scans found = rule_breasts(WATER_MIN, CENTRE_MIN) example_nova = next(n for n in analysis_novas if (n, "LEFT") in found and (n, "RIGHT") in found and sorted(found[n, s][0] for s in ("LEFT", "RIGHT")) == ["CANCER", "NORMAL"] and all(0 < found[n, s][2] < found[n, s][3] for s in ("LEFT", "RIGHT"))) plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 7 # small text so both panels fit side by side on an A4 page fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 4.3), sharey=True) x = np.linspace(2, 25, 600) sides = sorted(("LEFT", "RIGHT"), key=lambda side: found[example_nova, side][0] != "NORMAL") # NORMAL on the left for ax, side in zip(axes, sides): ax.set_box_aspect(1) # square panels label, ratio, n_usable, n_all = found[example_nova, side] good = [] for k, (nova, s_side, s_label, curve, height, centre) in enumerate(r for r in scan_records if r[0] == example_nova and r[1] == side): ok = usable(height, centre, WATER_MIN, CENTRE_MIN) tag = f"scan {k + 1}: water {height:.2f}, centre {centre:.1f}" if ok: good.append(curve) ax.plot(q, curve, color=ne.STATUS_COLOURS[label], lw=0.9, label=f"{tag}, usable") else: ax.plot(q, curve, color="grey", lw=0.8, ls="--", label=f"{tag}, rejected") with warnings.catch_warnings(): warnings.simplefilter("ignore", RuntimeWarning) mean_good = np.nanmean(good, axis=0) p = fit_two_gaussians(mean_good) for (height, centre, sigma), colour in ((p[:3], FAT_COLOUR), (p[3:], WATER_COLOUR)): within = (x >= centre - 3 * sigma) & (x <= centre + 3 * sigma) ax.fill_between(x[within], gaussian(x[within], height, centre, sigma), color=colour, alpha=0.25, lw=0) ax.plot(x, two_gaussians(x, *p), color="red", ls="--", lw=1.4, zorder=5, label="fit to the usable scans") ax.hlines(WATER_MIN, *WATER, color="black", lw=2.5, zorder=6, label=f"threshold: water peak {WATER_MIN:g}") ax.set(title=f"Nova {example_nova} {side}, {label}: {n_usable} of {n_all} scans usable\nWater:Fat = {ratio:.2f}", xlabel="q (nm⁻¹)", xlim=(2, 25)) ax.set_xticks([5, 10, 15, 20, 25]) ax.grid(alpha=0.3) ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=5.5, loc="upper left") axes[0].set_ylabel("I(q), stretched") axes[0].set_ylim(0, None) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 10 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The rule applied to one CANCER/NORMAL patient. Each panel is one breast: its usable scans (coloured) and the scans the rule rejects (grey, dashed), the threshold on the water peak (black bar over q 20-22), and the fat (yellow) and water (blue) Gaussians fitted to the mean of the usable scans, with their sum (red dashed).](on_the_fly_files/figure-html/fig-on-the-fly-example-output-1.png){#fig-on-the-fly-example width=767 height=422} ::: ::: The rule accepts 39% of all scans. The results using **only the usable scans**: | Usable scans | First-named breast higher | Median difference between the breasts, \|A − B\| | |---|---|---| | CANCER vs NORMAL | **15/18 \(83%\)** | 1\.00 | | BENIGN vs NORMAL | **10/27 \(37%\)** | 0\.66 | | CANCER vs BENIGN | **2/5 \(40%\)** | 2\.22 | | **NORMAL vs NORMAL** | – | **0\.58** (2 patients) | and the same comparisons using **only the scans the rule rejects**, the other 61% (each breast is the mean of its rejected scans, and a patient is compared only if both breasts have one): | Rejected scans | First-named breast higher | Median difference between the breasts, \|A − B\| | |---|---|---| | CANCER vs NORMAL | **11/23 \(48%\)** | 0\.13 | | BENIGN vs NORMAL | **16/31 \(52%\)** | 0\.12 | | CANCER vs BENIGN | **14/20 \(70%\)** | 0\.16 | | **NORMAL vs NORMAL** | – | **0\.08** (9 patients) | The **difference between the breasts** is |A − B| of the two breasts' Water:Fat, the median over the patients in each row. Because every curve is already normalised so its fat peak is 1, the absolute gap has a direct meaning and needs no further scaling. It does not need to know which breast is which, so it is what a blind measurement would see. **NORMAL vs NORMAL** is the baseline: how different two healthy breasts of the same patient are. If a cancer is to be spotted blind, a CANCER/NORMAL pair has to differ by clearly more than that. From the usable scans, the CANCER breast is the higher in **15/18 \(83%\)** of CANCER/NORMAL patients, and the two breasts differ by a median of **1\.00**. From the rejected, fatty scans it is the higher in only **11/23 \(48%\)**, about what chance would give, and the breasts differ by **0\.13**, close to the **0\.08** of two NORMAL breasts. Fatty scans cannot tell a CANCER breast from a NORMAL one; the information is in the water-rich scans. The NORMAL vs NORMAL baseline is thin, though: 2 patients have two NORMAL breasts with usable scans and 9 with rejected scans. ## Usable and rejected scans by age {#sec-usable-and-rejected-scans-by-age} Breasts are averaged within each age band, separately for NORMAL, BENIGN and CANCER, twice: once using only the scans that pass the test (usable), and once using only the scans it rejects. In each, a breast is the mean of the scans used. This shows what the kept and the discarded scans look like at different ages. ::: {#cell-fig-usable-by-age .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} plot_bands(summaries["usable"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![**Usable scans.** Mean prepared curve of NORMAL, BENIGN and CANCER breasts, one panel per age band (each breast is the mean of its usable scans), with ±1 SD across breasts shaded. The dashed line is the usable-scan water threshold over q 20–22.](on_the_fly_files/figure-html/fig-usable-by-age-output-1.png){#fig-usable-by-age width=767 height=293} ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-rejected-by-age .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} plot_bands(summaries["rejected"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![**Rejected scans.** As @fig-usable-by-age, but each breast is the mean of the scans the test rejects.](on_the_fly_files/figure-html/fig-rejected-by-age-output-1.png){#fig-rejected-by-age width=767 height=293} ::: ::: The table below sums this up: the mean water peak height (q 20–22) of each band's mean curve, with the number of breasts in brackets, each cell coloured on the heatmaps' scale (yellow high, dark blue low):
CohortScans usedunder 4040–4950 and over
NORMALusable0.66 (17)0.56 (26)0.53 (21)
NORMALrejected0.29 (12)0.21 (31)0.21 (59)
BENIGNusable0.73 (32)0.68 (55)0.56 (42)
BENIGNrejected0.22 (18)0.24 (43)0.20 (78)
CANCERusable0.59 (2)0.69 (19)0.60 (18)
CANCERrejected0.24 (2)0.25 (14)0.21 (35)
Breasts without an age are left out, and both figures share one y axis. The rejected scans look the same at every age and in every cohort, with a water peak near 0.2: once the water-bearing scans are taken out, what is left is fat, whatever the patient's age or label. The usable scans fall only a little with age, and CANCER stays about level while NORMAL and BENIGN drop, so in the older bands CANCER is the wettest. Only 2 CANCER breasts are under 40, so those curves say little. ::: {.callout-important title="Key result: we need to scan the glandular tissue"} The information is in the glandular/fibrous tissue, not in the fat. Using only the scans that reach glandular tissue (a real water peak), the CANCER breast has the higher Water:Fat in **15/18 \(83%\)** of CANCER/NORMAL patients; using only the fatty scans the rule rejects, it is **11/23 \(48%\)**, about what chance would give. The table of @sec-usable-and-rejected-scans-by-age shows why: the rejected scans have a water peak near 0.2 in every cohort and at every age, so they carry nothing that tells the cohorts apart, while the usable scans keep the differences. Whether a scan reaches glandular tissue depends mostly on breast density and age, and a breast's scans tend to all hit or all miss (@sec-glandular-details), so the scan protocol should make sure each breast is measured **in its glandular tissue**, moving to a clearly different spot when a scan shows no water peak. :::
